name: Ultrasound skin tightening

lead: Microfocused ultrasound, sold under names such as Ulthera, is used to lift sagging skin on the jawline, neck and brows without surgery.

Focused ultrasound heats tissue at set depths below the surface while sparing the outer skin; new collagen builds over the following months, tightening the area. Published studies include a rater-blinded cohort of the face and neck with brow lift as the main target, a single-treatment study of 22 Korean patients, a multiple-pass study of the lower face and neck, and a study of infraorbital laxity.

paras: It is performed by a clinician in a single session or a few sessions, with results developing gradually over months. It is also registered in trials on the arms.

Study introductions describe the safety profile of non-ablative tightening as good, though they note limited efficacy generally. Detailed adverse event data were not located, and results differ across studies.

angle.text: People use it to lift sagging skin on the jawline, neck and brows without surgery. Focused heat beneath the skin triggers new collagen over months, tightening the face and neck. Published cohort studies exist for face and neck.

lead: Ultrasound skin tightening uses intense focused ultrasound (IFUS), also called microfocused ultrasound (MFU), to deliver heat at chosen depths beneath the skin while sparing the surface. People use it to lift and firm sagging tissue on the brow, jawline, neck and under the chin without surgery, so the face reads as tighter and more defined.[1][2][3]

Branded systems such as Ulthera are used in registered trials on the face, neck and arms.[4] The technology was described in a 2014 review as the first energy-based skin lifting device cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration, specifically for lifting lax tissue on the neck, submentum and eyebrows.[3]

Published clinical studies include a rater-blinded prospective cohort study of the face and neck with brow lift as the main target, a single-treatment study in 22 Korean patients with blinded clinician assessment, a multiple-pass study of the lower face and neck, a study of infraorbital laxity, and a 2024 randomized blinded study of upper facial skin.[5][2][1][6][7] A 2025 paper examined a high-intensity parallel ultrasound variant.[8]
infobox: Face, neck, infraorbital area, upper arms, elbows
Described as minimal in the studies

paras: Treatment is performed by a clinician with a handheld device and a gel coupling medium; the studies describe topical anesthetic being applied beforehand and several probes with different frequencies and focal depths, for example 4 MHz at 4.5 mm and 7 MHz at 3.0 mm and 4.5 mm.[5] Treated areas in the literature include the forehead, temples, cheeks, submental region and sides of the neck.[5]
A distinctive feature highlighted in the 2014 review is that ultrasound allows direct visualization of the treated structures during treatment.[3]

IFUS produces thermal effects at different depths while sparing the overlying epidermis.[2] According to the 2014 review, coagulation is confined to arrays of roughly 1-mm3 zones that include the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and connective tissue, depositing energy in the deep dermal and subcutaneous layers.[3]

High-intensity focused ultrasound in general heats tissue at a focal point; Wikipedia notes tissue heated above 60 degrees Celsius for more than a second is irreversibly damaged.[9] A 2026 computational modelling paper proposes that efficacy of ultrasound tightening depends on fibroblast mechanotransduction, which it describes as impaired in obesity.[10]

A rater-blinded prospective cohort at a dermatology clinic assessed brow-lift efficacy in the context of full face and neck treatment, with standardized photographs at 2, 7, 28, 60 and 90 days and masked expert assessors comparing before and day-90 photographs. Its introduction notes that non-ablative tightening has an excellent safety profile that is mitigated by limited efficacy.[5]

A study of 22 Korean patients assessed safety and efficacy after a single IFUS session, using blinded clinicians and pathology.[2] A study of multiple-pass treatment evaluated lower face and neck laxity,[1] and another assessed infraorbital laxity as a non-surgical alternative to blepharoplasty, particularly for younger patients.[6]

A 2024 rater-blinded prospective study of 42 participants (37 women), 40 of whom completed 180 days of follow-up, treated the upper face with a newer microfocused ultrasound device and measured brow lift from photographs and three-dimensional vector analysis.[7] The 2014 review concluded ultrasound is a safe and efficacious treatment for mild skin tightening and lifting.[3]

Registered trials include combinations with thread lifting and with neck liposuction (the latter withdrawn), studies of the neck, elbows, upper arms and face using the Ulthera system, a long-term study using quantitative instruments, and an ongoing 273-participant trial of a high-intensity device for submental and neck laxity.[11][12][13][14][15]

Reports in the literature are mostly non-randomized or blinded-rater photograph studies with follow-up of weeks to months, so the size of lift is described in graded improvement scores or brow-height measurements rather than a single standard effect size; the 2024 randomized blinded study added three-dimensional vector analysis for this reason.[7][5]

Non-ablative tightening technologies are described in the literature as offering minimal downtime, discomfort and risk of adverse events.[5] The studies record pain, adverse events, physical findings and patient satisfaction ratings.[5]

Wikipedia's overview of focused ultrasound notes the general principle that tissue held above about 60 degrees Celsius for more than a second is irreversibly damaged, which is the thermal effect that cosmetic devices aim to confine to small deep zones while sparing the surface.[9] The 2014 review describes the technique as safe, concluding it is efficacious for mild skin tightening and lifting.[3]

A 2024 review of anti-aging trends in Australia lists radiofrequency and ultrasound skin tightening devices among widely used options, alongside lasers and injectables, and reports a surge in cosmetic procedures linked to video-call appearance and social media influence.[16]

A US survey of cosmetic physicians found that delegation of procedures to non-physician providers is common, and that rates differ between dermatologists and other specialties, relevant to who may actually operate such devices.[17]

timeline.event: Rater-blinded cohort study of ultrasound tightening of facial and neck skin published.[5]
Study of IFUS in Asian skin published; several Ulthera feasibility trials begin.[2][4]
Multiple-pass lower face/neck and infraorbital laxity studies published.[1][6]
Randomized blinded study of upper face brow lift published.[7]
